property_summary: If lockInGuess is called with any value != 1 ether it must revert (so caller cannot lock a guess unless they send exactly 1 ether).
Calling lockInGuess with any value other than 1 ether always reverts (so it only succeeds when exactly 1 ether is sent).
If lockInGuess call with value equal to 1 ether does not revert, then any call with a different value must revert (i.e., only exactly 1 ether is accepted).
If lockInGuess succeeds when sending amount X, then sending any different amount Y must revert (i.e., only the exact amount accepted by the contract can succeed).
lockInGuess succeeds exactly when the caller sends 1 ether (i.e., reverted is false iff amount == 1 ether).

For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) lockInGuess if and only if msg.value == 1 ether; the mutant tightens this to require msg.value == 2 ether, so for some fuzzed msg.value the reference accepts but the mutant rejects (or vice versa).

For any caller and any ether amount, the reference C accepts (does not revert) lockInGuess when msg.value == 1 ether and rejects otherwise; the mutant tightens the requirement to msg.value == 2 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where reference accepts but mutant reverts (or vice versa).

For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) lockInGuess when msg.value == 1 ether and thus successfully records the guess (making a subsequent getter reflect that state), whereas the mutant tightens the requirement to 2 ether and will reject (revert) for some msg.value inputs that the reference accepted.

For any caller and any guessed hash, calling lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether succeeds on the reference (records the guess and sets a nonzero block) whereas the mutant requires 2 ether and will revert for those same inputs, so the property: 'calling lockInGuess with 1 ether returns (does not revert)' holds for the reference for all inputs but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller and any bytes32 hash, calling lockInGuess(hash) with msg.value == 1 ether always succeeds (does not revert) and thus records a nonzero stored block for that caller; the mutant tightened the requirement to 2 ether and will revert for some inputs (e.g., when msg.value == 1 ether), breaking this rule.

For any caller and any hash, the reference contract C never allows a caller to overwrite an existing locked guess (lockInGuess reverts if caller already has a pending guess), while the mutant removes that check and therefore for some inputs allows overwriting an existing guess (i.e. lockInGuess succeeds twice for same caller), violating the uniqueness rule.

For any caller and guess hash, after lockInGuess is called with 1 ether the stored block number for that caller in the reference contract is strictly greater than the current block number at the time of the call (it's set to block.number + 1), whereas the mutant sets it equal to the current block number, breaking that invariant for some inputs.
